sections.body:
Power is the ability to make things happen. It comes from resources, from a position, from knowledge, from money, and from the people who are willing to act for you. Power does not need anybody's permission. If you can pay for it, order it, publish it, lock it or hire it, you have power, whatever the room thinks of you.

Authority is power the other side accepts. It is the right to be followed. Authority is not a property of the person: it is a relationship, and it exists only while the people who are followed keep granting it. The same person can hold authority in one room and none in another. The chief engineer is followed at the machine and not in the meeting about the schedule.

Legitimate authority is authority whose basis can be named, stated and questioned. It comes from a source everybody can see: knowledge that is current and checked, a role that carries a defined responsibility, or a rule that applies to everybody, including the person who uses it. When somebody asks *why should I follow this?*, legitimate authority has an answer that is not a threat and not a mood.

The difference matters at work. Power can be used without agreement; it has to be enforced, and it costs something every time. Authority runs on agreement, which is cheaper and steadier, and which can be withdrawn. So the question *who has the power here?* and the question *whose decision will be followed here?* do not always have the same answer, and the second one is the one that shapes a meeting.
examples: The manager had the power to sign the order; the team had the authority to follow it or not.
Authority was granted, not owned, so it could be withdrawn.
Legitimate authority has a reason you can hear: here is the rule, here is the evidence.
sections.heading: Power, authority, and the difference between them

terms.example: The power to shut the line down was in his hands, and it did not need anybody's permission.
terms.gloss: The ability to make things happen, whether or not the people affected agree.

terms.example: He had authority over the machine, and none over the schedule.
terms.gloss: Power that other people accept and act on: the right to be followed.

terms.example: It was legitimate authority: she showed the standard and said who had signed the rule.
terms.gloss: Authority whose basis can be named and questioned, such as checked knowledge, a defined role or a rule that applies to everybody.

sections.body:
Authority is claimed with a reason. There are five common bases, and it pays to know which one is in use, because each one is checked in a different way.

Expertise claims the right to be believed on the subject. The claim is strong while the knowledge is current, and it weakens the moment the field moves. It is the only base that can be tested by asking for the evidence: show me the measurement, the manual, the failure record. **Position** claims the right to decide because of the role. The role is lent, not owned: it comes with a responsibility that cannot be lent away, and it ends with the role. **Procedure** claims the right to decide because a rule says so. A rule is impersonal, which is its strength: it decides the same way for everybody, and it can be followed in public. A visible order is checkable; a hidden favour is not.

Reciprocity claims the right to be followed because something was given first: help, a favour, an introduction, a chance. It is the quietest of the five and the hardest to refuse, because refusing the decision also refuses the relationship. **Character** claims the right to be followed because of trust in the person: *you know I am not going to throw you under the bus*. It is the most fragile base, because nothing is written down and there is no document to point at.

Two words belong to this section. **Institutional power** is power that belongs to the office and not to the person: the badge, the account, the contract, the rulebook, the machine that only the duty holder may stop. It outlives the person who holds it and it works for whoever holds the office, which is why the person behind the badge still answers for what the office does. **Deference** is the behaviour that keeps authority in place: giving way, not arguing, accepting a decision on the title alone. Deference is normal and it is not weakness. It becomes a problem when it stops being a choice and nobody in the room is left who is allowed to choose.
examples: The authority came from the procedure, so the procedure can be seen.
The decision was his to make, and the responsibility stayed with him.
Institutional power belongs to the office; the answer still belongs to the person.
sections.heading: How authority is claimed and kept

terms.example: Institutional power is why the badge opens the door even though the badge is not the man.
terms.gloss: Power that belongs to an office or an organisation rather than to a person, and passes on with the role.

terms.example: Reciprocity was doing the work: the favour he had done last year settled the question.
terms.gloss: The exchange in which something given first creates a claim on what comes next.

terms.example: Deference is not weakness, but a room full of deference has nobody left to check anything.
terms.gloss: The habit of giving way to authority without asking for the reason.

sections.body:
These are the words used in workplace policy, in contracts, in safety rules and in the reports written after something has gone wrong. Learn them for two reasons: you can name what is happening, and you can use the name in writing.

Influence is the widest word of the set. It is any effect one person has on another: a request, an example, a piece of advice. Influence is not a privilege and not an abuse; it exists in every direction. **Persuasion** is influence that works on an open choice: the other person is free to say no and still gets the whole argument. **Coercion** is influence that takes the choice away, by force or by the threat of a cost — to your pay, to your safety, to your job, or to the safety of somebody close to you. Coercion leaves a trace, because it needs a threat.

Hierarchy is the arrangement that says who decides and who answers for it: the line of roles, the chain of command, the order of rank. A hierarchy is a design, not an accusation. The question is whether the roles at the top answer for the decisions taken in their name. **Mandate** is the formal authority to act inside a stated limit: the board's mandate, the mandate to negotiate, the mandate to sign up to a limit. A mandate answers *how far may I go*, and it is the word to look for when somebody asks you to go further than their role.

Next to it sits **sanction**, the consequence an institution attaches to an act: an approval, a penalty, a permission. *Sanction* is one of the words that changes meaning with the field around it. In law it is a penalty; in management it can be a green light; in trade it is a restriction. Read it in the sentence, never in the word alone.
examples: In writing: I am not refusing the decision. I am asking for the mandate behind it.
That is influence, not an order, and influence can be refused.
The hierarchy is the design; the question is who answers for a decision taken in it.
sections.heading: The words of the subject

terms.example: Influence is not a privilege: the newest member of the team influences the oldest one as well.
terms.gloss: Any effect one person has on another, from a request to advice, in either direction.

terms.example: That was persuasion: she explained the plan and left the decision to him.
terms.gloss: An attempt to win agreement in which the other person is free to say no.

terms.example: Sign the form today or lose the job — that is coercion, not persuasion.
terms.gloss: The removal of a real choice by force or by the threat of a cost to the other person.

terms.example: The hierarchy is clear on paper; the account, the invoice and the parts were not.
terms.gloss: The arrangement of roles that says who decides and who answers for the decision.

terms.example: His mandate was to negotiate the price, not to sign the contract.
terms.gloss: The formal authority to act, together with the limits that bound it.

sections.body:
Two kinds of authority look the same in a meeting: one person decides, and the others accept. The difference is not the amount of power and not the style of the person holding it. The difference is what happens to a question.

Legitimate authority can take a question and still hold the decision. Authority that avoids accountability cannot, because the question is exactly what would expose it: the decision was made for a reason that cannot be stated, or it protects the person who made it rather than the work.

Read the table as a set of checks that work on any decision, including your own. None of the columns asks you to judge a person. Each one asks what the decision is built on, and whether it can survive an answer.
examples: The reason was written down, so the decision could be checked later.
I asked for the basis, and the answer was that there was no basis to give.
The decision protected the person who made it, not the work.
sections.heading: Legitimate authority and authority that avoids accountability

rows: Where does the right come from?
From a basis that can be named: knowledge, a role, or a rule that applies to everybody.
From the holder alone: the title, the mood, or the fact that nobody is around to disagree.
Yes. The basis can be stated, checked and discussed, and the decision can still change.
No. The question is treated as insubordination, disloyalty or a bad attitude.
What happens when the answer is no?
The decision stands or is revised, and the reason is written down for the record.
The question is remembered, and the person is marked as difficult.
In the open, with the people affected present or invited.
In a corridor, in a private message, or by a decision that leaves no record.
A reason connected to the work: safety, cost, time, the customer, the standard.
A reason that cannot be checked: trust me, I know, that is how we do things here.
A named owner, who can be asked later what the decision was based on.
Nobody: the decision belongs to the position, and the position has no face.

terms.example: Transparency was missing: nobody could say which number the decision was based on.
terms.gloss: The condition that the reasons for a decision are visible and can be checked by the people affected.

sections.body:
Six questions, in this order. They work in a meeting, in a review, on the phone and in an email. The order matters: the first questions are cheap, and by the fifth one the room has usually told you what the decision really is.

Two words belong here. **Due process** is the set of rules a decision must follow: notice, the chance to be heard, a written reason, a way to appeal. A decision that follows due process survives an objection. A decision that skips it does not have to be wrong to be unsafe to argue with. **Accountability** is the answer that is owed for the decision: who answers, to whom, and when. Accountability is the opposite of authority — authority says *you will be followed*, accountability says *you will be asked*. A person can hold a lot of authority and very little accountability, and that combination is where a reader of this article should be most careful.

And the rule that protects you: object to the basis, not to the person. *I want to understand how the decision was made* is an objection. *You are not the right person to decide this* is an attack on the role, and the room closes against you. Keep the sentence attached to the decision, and keep it calm.
examples: On what basis is this the right decision?
Which information supports that? I would like to see it.
I am asking about the basis of the decision, not about the person who made it.
sections.heading: How to question authority without paying for it
steps: Ask for the basis: "On what basis is this the right decision?" Ask it as a request, in the neutral voice you would use for a date, not as an accusation.
Ask for the evidence: "Which information supports that?" The answer can be a measurement, a standard, a manual, a cost or a customer requirement, and any of them can be shown.
Ask what the decision is for: "What is this decision meant to achieve?" Write the aim down, because the effect can be compared with it later.
Ask who is affected: "Who does this change for?" Name the people who are not in the room, and ask whether they should be.
Ask what happens if the answer is no: "What happens if we do it another way?" This makes the cost of refusing visible, and it is often the question that moves the decision.

Put the objection in writing: after the meeting, send a short email that states the decision, the question and what you asked for. The record is the protection, and it is the start of the next step if no answer comes.

terms.example: Without due process the decision was final, and there was nowhere to take it.
terms.gloss: The rules a decision must follow: notice, the chance to be heard, a written reason and a way to appeal.

terms.example: He had the authority to sign it, and the accountability to explain it six months later.
terms.gloss: The answer that is owed for a decision: who answers, to whom, and when.

sections.body:
This article describes a mechanism. It does not tell you to refuse instructions, and it does not make every hierarchy illegitimate.

Hierarchy is not manipulation. A clear order from a named owner, with a reason you can hear and a record you can read, is legitimate authority even when you would have chosen differently. Refusing an order because you dislike it is insubordination, and the cost of that is yours. An objection is something else: it names the basis of the decision and asks for the evidence, and it accepts the decision if the basis holds. The difference is not courage. It is the target of the sentence.

It does not give you a test for a person either. Nothing here says that your manager, your client or your uncle is manipulating you, and this article supplies no way to find out. What it supplies is a way to ask about a decision, and the same questions work on your own decisions.

And it does not replace the law, the contract, the safety rule or the policy. Some authority cannot be questioned at the moment you want to question it: an emergency shutdown, a safety instruction, a legal obligation, a court order. In those cases the right to question comes later, in writing, through the process that exists for it.
examples: Hierarchy is not manipulation, and a clear order is still a legitimate order.
Refusing the order because you dislike it is insubordination, not objection.
An objection names the basis of the decision, and it accepts the answer.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
Use these at the moment you have to decide, not afterwards. The first three are for a meeting, the next two for a review or a one-to-one, and the last three for a message to a manager and for the case where the decision has already been made.

None of them needs a dramatic voice, and none of them refuses the decision. The point is to make the basis of a decision audible while there is still time to hear it.
examples: Before we go on, can you say what this decision is based on?
What is this decision meant to achieve?
Who does this change for? Are they in the room?
I would like to understand the standard this is measured against.
Which of these results changed the decision?
Thank you for the decision. I have two questions about the basis, and I will send them in writing.
I understand the decision is made. I would like to record my concern about the safety check.
Could we add the reason for this to the minutes, please?
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
When nobody has a title, the power does not disappear; it moves. It goes to the person who holds the information, to the person who holds the relationships, to the person who acts first, and to the person with the loudest channel. The first three are power in the ordinary sense. The fourth is usually noise.

A team without a manager has an informal hierarchy: the person others go to when something is stuck. That person usually has power because they fix things, or because they know where things are, not because they talk most. The **deference** of the team keeps that informal hierarchy in place, and it works well as long as the informal leader can be questioned like anybody else. When the informal leader cannot be questioned, the team has an invisible boss, and nobody can appeal, because there is no rule that says what to appeal to.

A family works the same way. The person who keeps the calendar, the money and the connections holds real power, and nobody elected them. In an online space, the person with the largest audience holds the power to set the terms of the conversation, and the terms are usually written by whoever wrote the tool. Being the loudest is not authority, but it is close enough to be mistaken for it.

The institutional power is still there in all three cases. The rulebook, the contract, the code of conduct and the process do not need anybody in charge to exist, and they are what you point at when nobody answers a question. Where the informal power and the institutional power agree, the group is calm. Where they disagree and the informal side wins every time, the answer is not a louder voice: it is a question asked in the right place, by somebody with something at stake in the answer.
examples: The loudest channel is not the authority; the person who knows where the parts are usually is.
The informal leader led the team, and the team still asked the informal leader why.
There is no manager, but there is still a process, and the process can be pointed at.
sections.heading: Where power sits when nobody is in charge

item.summary: Power is the ability to make things happen; authority is power the other side accepts. After reading this you can tell the two apart, name the five bases on which authority is claimed, test whether a decision can be questioned, and raise an objection in a meeting, in a review or in writing without turning the difference into insubordination.
item.title: Power Dynamics and Authority Manipulation
